plain: Obsidian is a program for writing notes that save as plain text files inside a folder on your computer. Picture an old library's card catalog: each note is a card, folders are the drawers, and links are colored threads connecting cards to one another. Nobody keeps a copy on some distant company's servers: if Obsidian shut down tomorrow, your notes would still be there and you could open them with Notepad. What sets it apart from a real card catalog is that pulling a thread jumps you to the other card instantly, and each card tells you on its own who has mentioned it.

account.free: The program is free with no note limit for personal use. No account, no 30-day trial, no cap on anything: you download it and that's it. The community plugins recommended here (Templater, Dataview, Kanban) are free too. You only pay for the company's own extras: syncing between phone and computer with their official service runs about $4 a month paying for a full year, and publishing notes as a website runs about $8 a month. If you use it to work inside a company of more than two people, the commercial license runs about $50 a year per person. Prices are set in dollars and change from time to time: check obsidian.md/pricing before paying anything, don't trust this figure.
steps: Go to obsidian.md. The big button in the center says 'Download' and it already detects that you're on Windows. It's a bit under 100 MB. Notice what it does NOT ask for: no email, no password, no card. There's no sign-up because there's nothing to sign up for.
Install it and don't panic at the blue warning

When you open the downloaded file, Windows might show a blue screen saying 'Windows protected your PC'. It happens with almost any program that doesn't come from the Microsoft Store. Check that where it says publisher it reads Obsidian, click 'More info' and then 'Run anyway'.
Create the vault and choose carefully where it lives

The first screen gives you three options. The top one, 'Create new vault', is yours: type a name like 'AI Project' and use 'Browse' to choose the folder on disk. Two rules: the path shouldn't contain special characters, and don't put it inside another vault you already have. That folder becomes your entire archive: what you put in it are notes, what you take out stops being visible.
Set up all the folders at once, before writing anything

In the left-hand column, hover over the vault's name: small icons appear. The folder icon with a plus sign creates a new folder. Create these eight and put a number in front so they sort themselves: 00-Inbox, 10-Projects, 20-Prompts, 30-Decisions, 40-Errors, 50-Resources, 90-Templates, 99-Archive. It takes two minutes and saves you the reorganization three months from now.
Turn on the built-in plugins that actually matter

Ctrl+comma opens 'Settings'. In the left column, 'Core plugins': these come bundled with Obsidian, nothing to download. Turn on 'Templates', 'Daily notes', 'Backlinks', 'Outgoing links', 'Tags view', 'Quick switcher', and above all 'File recovery', which saves copies of every note every few minutes in case you mess something up.
Tell it where the templates are

Still in 'Settings'. Scroll down to 'Templates' in the left column and in 'Template folder location' type 90-Templates. If you skip this, later on you'll get a notice saying it can't find any template and won't understand why.
Write, link, and verify from outside

Ctrl+N creates a note. Give it a normal, human name: 'My candle shop - dashboard'. Inside, type two brackets in a row, [[, and choose another note: you've just created a link. Now open Windows Explorer and go to the folder: there's a .md file for every note, and they're plain text. Open one with Notepad and you'll see your link in brackets. That's the proof the notes are yours.
account.warning: There's no safety net here, and that's the flip side of everything being yours. Your notes are on your disk and nowhere else. If the disk dies, if you delete the folder without looking, or if you reformat your computer, there's no company you can ask for a copy, because nobody else has one. It's irreversible: there's no undo button for that. Before you put anything in there that matters to you, decide where the backup goes, and turn on 'File recovery' in the settings.

first: Create the eight numbered folders before writing your first note. Structure first, content later: the other way around turns into a reorganization.
Create the index note for your project in 10-Projects, with the exact name of what you're building: 'My Candle Shop'. It's going to be your homepage for months.

Write three real notes and link them to the index with [[: a prompt you already use in 20-Prompts, a decision made in 30-Decisions, and an error you've hit in 40-Errors. Then look at the index note's right-hand panel, under Backlinks: all three show up on their own, and you never wrote that list.
Set up the backup today, not tomorrow: put the folder inside OneDrive or Dropbox, or put a reminder in your calendar to drag it to an external drive every Friday.
Learn three shortcuts and stop researching: Ctrl+O opens a note by its name, Ctrl+N creates one, Ctrl+Shift+F searches a word across all of them.
shortcuts: Opens any note by typing three letters of its name. It's by far the shortcut you'll use the most every day: it replaces browsing through folders. If your notes are named the way you'd say them out loud, you always get it right on the first try.

The command palette: a search box for everything the program knows how to do. Type two words ('template', 'graph', 'export') and it offers it to you. Good so you don't have to memorize any shortcut beyond these ten.
New note in whatever folder you're in. Use it the moment an idea crosses your mind; you'll file it away later.

Two brackets in a row inside the text: the list of your notes opens and you choose. This isn't just any shortcut, it's Obsidian's central gesture. If you type a name that doesn't exist yet, the note gets created the day you click the link.
Searches a word across all your notes at once, not just the open one. This is how you'll find 'that Stripe error I already solved back in March'.
Switches between edit mode and reading mode. In reading mode you see the note clean, as it would look published; in edit mode you see the symbols. Use it to reread without distractions.
Opens that note in a new tab beside the current one, without losing what you had. Essential for keeping the prompt on the left and the result on the right while talking to the AI.
Renames the open note and, very importantly, goes into every note that linked to it and fixes the name. Always rename from here, never from Windows Explorer.
Opens 'Settings'. This is where you turn on plugins, change the templates folder, and assign new shortcuts.

Back and forward, like in a browser: returns to the previous note after jumping through three links. Note: this shortcut has changed between versions, and in some it's Ctrl+Alt+arrow. Check it in 'Settings' then 'Hotkeys' by searching for 'Navigate back'.
daily: Everything that crosses your mind goes into 00-Inbox without a second thought. Ctrl+N, write it, close it. Once a week, empty that folder by moving each note to its place or deleting it. Without an inbox, you hesitate about where to save something and end up not saving it at all.

Link as you write, not afterward. Every time you mention your project, a prompt, or a tool, type [[ and choose it. It costs a second and it's the only thing separating this from a folder full of forty loose files.
One note per prompt that works, in 20-Prompts, with the exact text you pasted and the model you used. This folder is the most valuable part of your vault: it's your work, not the AI's.
Every error you hit goes to 40-Errors with the message copied LITERALLY and what fixed it. Errors repeat two months later and you won't remember.

Few folders, lots of links. If you're torn between two folders, the note goes to the more obvious one and you link it from wherever it's needed. A note can be linked from ten places, but it only lives in one folder.

Tags only for status, never for topic. #active, #stalled, #done, #working, #broken. Links already handle the topic. If you start with #website #shop #payments you'll end up with a hundred and twenty tags and none of them useful.

A daily note for the project with Ctrl+P and 'Daily note': three lines on what you tried today, what failed, and what's next for tomorrow. In a month you'll have your project's diary without ever having written a diary.

templates.name: A vibecoding vault ready in five minutes: folders, rules, and index note
templates.what: The complete folder structure for someone building something by talking to AI, plus the index note that acts as the project's homepage. Works from week one and holds up to two hundred notes without needing to change.
templates.how:
1. In the left column, hover over your vault's name and click the folder icon with a plus sign.
2. Create the eight folders from the list below, with the number and dash in front. The number isn't decoration: it forces them to sort the way you want instead of alphabetically.
3. Go into 10-Projects, press Ctrl+N, and name the note with the real name of what you're building.
4. Copy the index note block and paste it inside.
5. Replace what's in brackets with your own. Leave the [[names in double brackets]] as they are: they're links, and ones pointing to notes that don't exist yet will show in a dimmer color until you create them.
6. Pin that note: right-click on its tab and choose 'Pin'. That way it never closes on you.
fill: [PROJECT NAME]
What you're building, said the way you'd tell your mother: 'Handmade candle shop'.
[WHAT IT DOES, IN ONE SENTENCE]
What it's for and who it's for. If it doesn't fit in one sentence, you don't have it clear yet.
[TOOLS]
What you're building it with: Claude, Cursor, Lovable, Supabase, Vercel, whatever applies.
[MONTHLY SPEND]
What it's actually costing you in dollars per month, adding up every subscription. Write it even if it's $0.
[NEXT STEP]
The one thing you're going to do tomorrow. One. Not a list of nine.
templates.code:
FOLDER STRUCTURE (create these in Obsidian, exactly as shown)

00-Inbox/          Everything that crosses your mind and you don't know where it goes. Emptied every week.
10-Projects/       One index note per project. It's the cover page.
20-Prompts/        One prompt per note. Your treasure.
30-Decisions/      What you decided and why. The why gets forgotten in ten days.
40-Errors/         The literal error message and what fixed it.
50-Resources/      Prices, links, screenshots, outside things.
90-Templates/      The templates. Configured in Settings > Templates.
99-Archive/        The dead stuff. Not deleted, just set aside.

----------------------------------------------------------------
INDEX NOTE (paste this into a new note in 10-Projects)
----------------------------------------------------------------

---
type: project
status: active
monthly_spend: [MONTHLY SPEND]
tags: [project]
---

# [PROJECT NAME]

**What it is:** [WHAT IT DOES, IN ONE SENTENCE]
**Built with:** [TOOLS]
**Monthly cost:** [MONTHLY SPEND]

## Next step
- [ ] [NEXT STEP]

## Prompts that work
- [[Prompt - build the homepage]]
- [[Prompt - connect the contact form]]

## Decisions made
- [[Decision - why I'm not using WordPress]]
- [[Decision - where I store orders]]

## Errors solved
- [[Error - the site shows blank when published]]

## Where everything is
- Code: [paste your computer's folder path here]
- Published site: [paste the address here]
- Passwords: NO. Not here. They go in a password manager.

templates.name: Template for a prompt that works
templates.what: A record for every prompt that gave you a good result, with the exact text, the model, and what went wrong on previous attempts. It's what lets you repeat a win three months later instead of fighting from scratch again.
templates.how:
1. Go to the 90-Templates folder and press Ctrl+N. Name the note 'Prompt Template'.
2. Paste the block below into it and close the note. Don't touch it again.
3. Check in Ctrl+comma, under 'Templates', that 'Template folder location' says 90-Templates.
4. Now, every time you want to save a prompt: Ctrl+N while in the 20-Prompts folder, name it something like 'Prompt - build the homepage', and with the note open and empty press Ctrl+P, type 'Insert template', and choose 'Prompt Template'.
5. If you're going to do this ten times a day, assign it a shortcut: Ctrl+comma, 'Hotkeys', search for 'Insert template' and click the plus icon to record whatever combination you want.
6. The {{date:YYYY-MM-DD}} converts itself to today's date automatically when inserting the template. It's from the built-in 'Templates' plugin, no need to install anything.
fill: project
The exact name of your index note, in double brackets and quotes. If it doesn't match letter for letter, the link won't connect.
model
Which AI you used: Claude Opus, GPT-5, Gemini. Matters, because the same prompt doesn't perform the same across two models.
status
working, partial, or discarded. Nothing more. Three states, not seven.
THE WHOLE PROMPT
The exact text you pasted, typos and all. Don't summarize or improve it: if you summarize it, it stops working and you won't know why.
What failed before
The attempts that didn't land. Worth more than the one that did work, because it saves you from repeating them.
templates.code:
---
type: prompt
project: "[[Exact name of your project]]"
model: Claude
status: working
created: {{date:YYYY-MM-DD}}
tags: [prompt]
---

# {{title}}

## What it's for
One sentence. What I ask it and what it gives back.

## The whole prompt
```
THE WHOLE PROMPT, PASTED AS-IS, UNEDITED
```

## What needs to change before using it
- [DETAIL 1] -> what to replace it with
- [DETAIL 2] -> what to replace it with

## What failed before
- Attempt 1: what I asked for and what went wrong.
- Attempt 2: what I asked for and what went wrong.

## Related
- [[Error - ...]]
- [[Decision - ...]]

templates.name: Session template: a diary of what you talk about with the AI
templates.what: One note per work session. Three minutes when you finish, and a month later you have the project's complete history: what you tried, what cost money, and where you left off. Good for picking back up on Monday without wasting half an hour trying to remember.
templates.how:
1. Turn on the built-in 'Daily notes' plugin under Ctrl+comma, 'Core plugins'.
2. Inside 'Daily notes', set 'New file location' to 10-Projects, and 'Template file location' to 90-Templates/Session Template.
3. Create the 'Session Template' note in 90-Templates and paste the block below.
4. Every day, Ctrl+P and type 'Daily note': it creates today's note already filled in with the template.
5. Fill it in at the END of the session, not the beginning. At the start you don't know anything yet.

One sentence, written before opening the AI.

templates.name: The five plugins that are actually worth it (and the automatic dashboard)
templates.what: Of the thousand-plus community plugins, these five solve something real. The Dataview panel turns your vault into a dashboard that updates itself: working prompts, active projects, orphan notes, and pending tasks, without you keeping a single list by hand.
templates.how:
1. Ctrl+comma to open settings. Under 'Community plugins' click 'Turn on community plugins' and accept the warning.
2. Click 'Browse' and search for and install only these, one at a time, with 'Install' then 'Enable':
   - Dataview: builds automatic lists and tables from your notes. It's what powers the dashboard below.
   - Templater: real templates, with date, time, and prompts when inserting them. The built-in plugin falls short once you pick up speed.
   - Kanban: drag-and-drop card boards, Trello-style, saved as an ordinary text note.
   - Omnisearch: a much better search than the default one; finds things even if you mistype.
   - Smart Connections or Copilot: adds an AI chat inside Obsidian that reads your notes. MONEY WARNING: Copilot asks for your own API key and every question gets billed to the provider, cents that add up. Smart Connections can run on your computer for free, but it's slow on ordinary laptops. Save this one for last.
3. Create a new note called 'Dashboard' in 10-Projects and paste the block below.
4. Switch it to reading mode with Ctrl+E: the tables fill themselves in. In edit mode you'll only see the query text, and that's normal.
5. Pin that note by right-clicking its tab and choosing 'Pin'.
WARNING: every plugin is a program written by a stranger that can read every file in your vault. Install these five and stop. Don't install twenty just because a video told you to.
fill: FROM "20-Prompts"
The exact name of your folder, quotes included. If your folder is named differently, change it here or the table will come out empty.
status = "working"
The word you use in your notes. It has to match letter for letter what you wrote in the properties.
monthly_spend
The name of the property you used in your project notes. If you named it differently, change it.
contains(file.folder, "90-Templates")
The folder you want the dashboard to ignore. Templates aren't orphan notes, they're templates.
templates.code:
# Dashboard

## Active projects

```dataview
TABLE status AS "Status", monthly_spend AS "$/month", file.mtime AS "Touched"
FROM "10-Projects"
WHERE type = "project"
SORT file.mtime DESC
```

## Prompts that work

```dataview
TABLE model AS "Model", file.mtime AS "Touched"
FROM "20-Prompts"
WHERE status = "working"
SORT file.mtime DESC
```

## Errors from the last 30 days

```dataview
LIST
FROM "40-Errors"
WHERE file.ctime >= date(today) - dur(30 days)
SORT file.ctime DESC
```

## Pending tasks across all notes

```dataview
TASK
WHERE !completed
GROUP BY file.link
```

## Orphan notes (nobody links to them: connect them or send to 99-Archive)

```dataview
LIST
WHERE length(file.inlinks) = 0
  AND !contains(file.folder, "90-Templates")
  AND !contains(file.folder, "99-Archive")
SORT file.name ASC
```

errors: You're trying to rename a note to a name another note already has, or save two identical notes in the same folder. Obsidian doesn't allow two files with the same name in the same folder, same as Windows. Give it a more specific name ('Prompt - homepage v2') or check with Ctrl+O first whether you'd already written it. Watch out: often the note that already exists is the good one and you were about to duplicate work.
You click a link and instead of opening the note it creates an empty one

The link was pointing to a name that doesn't exist: either there's a one-letter typo, or you renamed the note from Windows Explorer instead of with F2 inside Obsidian. Links with no destination show in a dimmer color than normal ones. Fix: delete the empty note that was just created, go back to the broken link, delete it, and type it again with [[ choosing from the list. And from now on, always rename with F2.
Files appear on their own named 'note-DESKTOP-4F3K9.md' or 'note (conflicted copy).md'

That's OneDrive, Dropbox, or iCloud warning you it found two different versions of the same note and doesn't know which is right. Happens when you edit on your computer and your phone almost at the same time, or when your computer shuts down mid-sync. Open both files, see which has the good text, copy anything missing into the good one, and delete the copy. To stop it repeating: fully close Obsidian before leaving, and wait for the cloud icon to turn green before opening it on the other device.

A plugin has broken, almost always after an Obsidian update or the plugin's own update. The vault works the same, you only lose what that plugin did. Go to Ctrl+comma, 'Community plugins', and turn it off with the switch. If it was Dataview, all your dashboards will show blank until it's back: that's normal, your notes are untouched. Try clicking 'Check for updates' on that same screen.
Templater Error: Template file not found

You asked it to insert a template and it can't find the file. It's almost always that the templates folder path is written wrong in the settings: an extra slash, a missing capital letter, or you typed 'Templates' when the folder is called '90-Templates'. Go to Ctrl+comma, find Templater (or Templates if you're using the built-in one) and type the path exactly as it appears in the left column, no slash at the start or end.
Dataview: No results to show for table query.

The query is written correctly but finds no note matching what you're asking for. Three causes, in order of frequency: the folder name in quotes doesn't match the real one; the property you're looking for (status, model, type) isn't written on any note yet; or the value doesn't match letter for letter, and 'Working' with a capital letter is not the same as 'working'. Open a note that should show up and check that it has those properties right at the top.
You open Obsidian and no notes appear, the left column is empty

It's almost never that they've been deleted. Usually you've opened a different vault, or the folder got moved (typical after putting it inside OneDrive later). Click the vault icon at the bottom left, 'Open another vault', and check the list. If your folder isn't where it used to be, use 'Open folder as vault' and point to where it is now. Before touching anything else, check in Windows Explorer whether the .md files are still on disk: if they are, you haven't lost anything.
You paste an image and the note only shows the text ![[photo.png]]

The image isn't where the note thinks it is. If you dragged the file in from the desktop and then moved or deleted it, the link points at nothing; Obsidian stores a link, not a copy inside the note. Fix the source: in Ctrl+comma, 'Files and links', set 'Default location for new attachments' to a specific folder and type 50-Resources. From then on, anything you paste gets copied into your vault automatically and stops depending on your desktop.

prompts.name: Design your vault's structure around your project
prompts.prompt: Act as someone who has spent years organizing notes in Obsidian and has also guided people without any technical background. I don't know how to code and I'm not planning to learn: I build things by asking AI in English, copying what it gives back, and testing it. I'm building [DESCRIBE WHAT YOU'RE BUILDING: A WEBSITE, A SHOP, AN APP, AN ASSISTANT] and I work [ALONE / WITH ONE OTHER PERSON]. I put in about [NUMBER] hours a week and I've been at it for [TIME]. The things I need to remember without fail are [LIST: prompts that work, prices, service passwords, decisions, errors, loose ideas]. Design the folder structure for my Obsidian vault with these conditions: eight top-level folders maximum, no subfolders at first, numbered names so they sort themselves, and for each folder one sentence saying exactly what goes in and what does NOT. Also tell me what five tags I should use and why those and not others, knowing I want status tags, not topic tags. Add a clear rule for deciding, when I'm torn between two folders, which one a note goes in. Finish with the three notes I should create today, with their exact names. Answer in plain English, casually, with short sentences, and don't use any technical word without translating it in parentheses the first time. Don't give me theory about named organization methods: give me folders and rules.

prompts.name: Have the AI generate the whole vault as ready-to-paste files
prompts.prompt: I need you to generate the initial content of my Obsidian vault as text files I can create by hand by copying and pasting. I don't know how to code. I work like this: I ask you for things in English, you give me back text, I copy and paste it. My project is [DESCRIBE THE PROJECT IN TWO SENTENCES] and I'm building it with [TOOLS YOU USE: Claude, Cursor, Lovable, Supabase, whatever applies]. Give me between eight and twelve notes, and for each one: first, the exact file name as I should type it in Obsidian, without the .md ending, and then the complete content in Markdown format, ready to paste all at once. Mandatory rules: every note must start with a properties block between three dashes at the top and three at the bottom, with at least type, status, and tags. Every note must link to at least two others using double brackets, and the names inside the brackets must match letter for letter the file names you've given me, otherwise the link won't connect. Names should be phrases I'd say out loud, not codes or abbreviations. No special characters in file names. Be sure to include a project index note, two prompt notes, two decision notes, and one error note. At the end, give me the list of folders where I should place each one. Plain English, casual tone, short sentences.

prompts.name: Get the automatic Dataview dashboard without knowing how to write queries
prompts.prompt: I want an automatic control panel inside Obsidian using the Dataview plugin, and I have no idea how to write queries and I'm not planning to learn the syntax. Explain it to me as you would to someone who doesn't code. My notes are organized like this: [PASTE YOUR LIST OF FOLDERS HERE]. The properties I write at the top of my notes, between three dashes, are [LIST: type, status, model, project, monthly_spend, date] and the values I use are [LIST THE EXACT VALUES: active, stalled, working, discarded]. I want a dashboard with these blocks: [SAY WHAT YOU WANT TO SEE: active projects, working prompts sorted by date, errors from the last month, unfinished tasks across all notes, notes nobody links to]. Give me the complete content of a single note called Dashboard, with its headings and query blocks, ready to paste all at once. Under each block, write me one plain-language line saying what it does, and which exact word I need to change if my folders are named differently. Warn me about the three mistakes that'll make a table come out empty, because I'd rather know that up front than fight with it for half an hour. Also remind me what the filled-in dashboard looks like, because in edit mode I only see the text. Plain English, casual tone, short sentences, no untranslated technical words.

prompts.name: Audit your vault once it's gotten out of hand
prompts.prompt: I have an Obsidian vault with about [NUMBER] notes and it's getting out of hand: I create new folders every other day, I have notes I can't find, and I don't know which ones are orphaned. I want you to act as an outside reviewer, no mercy and no sugarcoating. Here's the information: my list of folders is [PASTE IT], the list of my note names is [PASTE IT], and the tags I use are [PASTE THEM]. I don't know how to code and I don't want solutions that involve writing code or installing ten plugins. Tell me, in this order: first, which folders are redundant and which they should be merged with, one by one, with the reason; second, which notes have bad names, and give me the exact new name for each, knowing that a good name is one I'd say out loud and that also has to work when I type three letters into the search box; third, which tags are duplicating what folders or links already do and should be removed; fourth, which five new notes I'm clearly missing given what I already have. Order everything by what's doing the most damage right now. Warn me about which changes are irreversible and which I should back up before making. Finish with a thirty-minute plan: what to touch today and what to leave for later. Plain English, casual tone, short sentences.

words: Vault

The folder on your computer where all of a project's notes live. It's nothing magic: it's an ordinary folder that Obsidian looks at as a whole. You can have several vaults and they don't see each other.
Markdown

A way of formatting text by typing symbols by hand: two asterisks around a word and it comes out bold, a hash at the start of a line and that line is a heading. Even if the program disappears, you can still read the file perfectly.
Link between notes ([[ ]])
You type another note's name between two double brackets and it becomes clickable, like the underlined name of a menu item that takes you to another page. Clicking it jumps you to that note.
Backlinks
The list of notes pointing to the one you're reading. You don't write it or maintain it: it shows up on its own. It's the question 'who has mentioned me?' answered before you even asked it.
Tag (#tag)
A word with a hash in front that you stick inside a note to mark it. Good for the state of things (#active, #done), not for the topic: links already handle the topic.
Properties (frontmatter)

The block at the very top of a note, between three dashes at the top and three at the bottom, with loose data like status, model, or date. It's the note's ID card, and it's what lets automatic dashboards find it.
Template
An empty note with the blanks already in place that you copy every time you start another one like it. Like preprinted office forms: you just fill in the spaces.
Plugin

An add-on you plug into the program to make it do something it didn't do out of the box, like the attachments you put on a drill. The built-in ones are written by Obsidian; the community ones, by strangers.
Dataview
A plugin that reads the properties across all your notes and builds lists and tables that update themselves. It's like a spreadsheet formula, but applied to your notes.
Orphan note
A note that no link points to. It exists, but you only reach it by deliberately searching for it, so in practice it's lost.
matters: Nobody backs you up. A laptop's disk dies without warning, and the day it does, it takes the eight months of prompts you'd been refining with it. Copy the folder somewhere else even if it's crude, dragging it to an external drive once a week, and turn on 'File recovery' in the settings so you can rescue a note you wrecked yourself.

Few folders, lots of links, in that order. What sinks a vault isn't having a thousand notes, it's having forty folders and not knowing which one the note you're writing belongs in. With eight folders you never hesitate more than two seconds, and everything else is handled by links, which really can be infinite.

Name notes the way you'd say them out loud, and always rename with F2 from inside the app. A link is written by name, so 'Meeting summary prompt' shows up the moment you type 'summary'. You'll never reach 'Note 17'. And if you rename from Windows Explorer, every link pointing to that note breaks at once, without warning.

The fact that these are text files on your disk is exactly what makes this fit into an AI project. You can tell an assistant running on your computer 'read the 20-Prompts folder and tell me which ones look similar' and it reads all of them, no exporting, no copy-pasting, and no asking any company for permission. With a tool that keeps your notes on its own server, that path doesn't exist.
ignore: The graph view. It's the image that shows up in every video, and with twelve notes it tells you absolutely nothing. Come back to it once you have two hundred.

The thousand community plugins, the themes, and the appearance tweaks. Install the four recommended here and stop. Every plugin is a program written by a stranger that runs with access to every file in your folder, and none of them writes your notes for you.

The named methods (Zettelkasten, PARA, and company). They're ways of organizing notes that people defend as if they were football teams. They work, but building a system for an organization problem you don't have yet is a wasted afternoon.

questions.prompt: You've been writing for two weeks. You have a note called 'Meeting summary prompt' and you've linked to it from three other notes in the project. Today you realize the name is too short and you want to rename it 'Meeting summary prompt v3'. What happens to those three links?

options.text: You rename the note from inside Obsidian, and it goes into the other three and fixes the name for you.
options.why: Obsidian keeps track of who points to whom, so when you rename it, it uses that list, opens those three files, and rewrites the link text. The nuance that makes this correct is 'from inside Obsidian': if you rename the file from Windows Explorer with the program closed, nobody tells anyone, and all three links stay pointing to a name that no longer exists.

options.text: The three links break and you have to open the notes one by one and fix them by hand.
options.why: It's what's always happened to you with any link you've pasted anywhere, which is why it sounds like an uncomfortable truth. It breaks exactly at the point where the program does keep track of the relationship between notes and uses it to fix things on its own. That said: this is exactly what happens if you make the name change from outside.

options.text: It won't let you rename a note that has links pointing to it; you have to remove the links first.
options.why: Sounds like a sensible precaution, the kind of 'you can't delete this because it's in use' message you've seen a thousand times. But there's no delicate system to protect here: these are text files, and the note's name is the file's name. You rename whenever you want, as many times as you want.

questions.explain: A note's name is its address, and Obsidian only updates addresses while you make the change from inside the app.

questions.prompt: You have forty notes on the project: working prompts, what each model costs you, decisions made and why. You want an AI assistant running on your computer to summarize everything you decided in June. How do you get it that data?

options.text: You tell it which folder on the disk they're in and it reads them as-is.
options.why: They're ordinary text files in an ordinary folder, so any program able to open files reads them with no conversion, no exporting, and no permission from anyone. The important nuance: the assistant sees everything in that folder, not just what you had in mind, so point it at the project folder and not at all your documents.

options.text: You export them one by one to PDF and upload them.
options.why: It's the reflex office software has trained into you, where the real file is in a format only its own program understands and has to be converted to get it out. Here that step is unnecessary and actually gets in the way: turning text into PDF makes it worse, because you then have to pull the text back out of the PDF.

options.text: You have to connect your Obsidian account to the assistant and grant permission.
options.why: It's how almost everything else you've used works, so it's a completely reasonable question. It breaks on a detail that's hard to believe at first: there's no account to connect. You can use Obsidian for years without ever signing up, because there's no server holding your notes. The door in isn't an account, it's a folder.

questions.explain: If your notes are text files on your disk, you don't need an integration with anyone: you need to tell the tool where to look.
